utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. When we adjourned the last time, Mr. Milovancevic, you had indicated that you had only just received some bulk of documents from the Prosecution which could possibly be Rule 68 material and you wanted to go through that material to be able to tell us what the Defence's position is on that material. Are you able to give us any answers?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Your Honour, give you some answers. We looked through the documents. They were rather extensive documents, most of them we had already had in our possession, but it was non-selective material and -- relating to different topics, so we needed quite a lot of time to establish what referred to what. But we have completed our task, and we're not asking for any deadlines or anything like that from the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's very comforting to hear, Mr. Milovancevic. And then let me deal with a few other housekeeping matters that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, I believe you would be the counsel for the OTP dealing with this matter or would it be another counsel? Because there's an issue that I wish to raise with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. No, it's me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Notwithstanding what learned counsel for the Defence has said, having regard to the position and the provisions of Rule 68(i), why is it that the material itself was being served at the 11th hour, after the close, virtually or just at the point of closure of the case, in terms evidence. Could we hear from you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The answer to that is that the Prosecution is constantly reviewing material to look for Rule 68 and it comes up in a variety of ways. We do – we -- when we start the Rule 68 process, we do a number of searches called ISU searches --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: ISU meaning?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I was afraid you would ask that. It's some computer unit -- it's a computer unit that we have that has the ability to search through all of the documents in the OTP collection and print out documents that contain a key word, for example. So it stands for something like -- that has to do with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. Something like that. And so what we do is we come up with a number of key words, and in this case the Defence was aware what the key words were, the accused's name, of course, but also the names of various witnesses and so forth. The OTP, of course, is constantly receiving new information, new documents, you know, I wouldn't say on a daily basis but virtually on a daily basis. New collections, new documents come in, new things are received. So what we do is we update those searches periodically, and then we conduct reviews of the update searches. What we also -- when we get new witnesses or new information, we do new searches. For example, we did a search on each Defence witness, and we would review the results of those searches, and those searches would be done literally days before the witness testified. The reviews would be done before the witness testified, and then we would conduct those reviews and we would turn over Rule 68 information. So in other words, we -- throughout the Defence case, we were constantly reviewing material and turning it over. Now, one thing that obviously happens is that a lot of material is reviewed again and -- the same material is reviewed again and again and again, which is why Mr. Milovancevic was able to say that much of what he had received, he had already received or already was in possession or was already available to him. So that's the answer to your question. And of course the Prosecution's position on this is, had there been any significant material -- and this is, frankly, a process that will continue. Our obligation under Rule 68 continues beyond today, and in the event information is obtained by us or discovered by us or learned by us, that is Rule 68, we will immediately turn it over. And generally our position is that if the Defence wants to make that available to the Trial Chamber, if it is significant, if it could have any effect on the case, we would not oppose that being made available to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation, Mr. Whiting, because the Trial Chamber was excited by two aspects, the issue of the time, having regard to the rule, as well as the volume, which you have put in the context and explained. And we're certainly very grateful for that. Thank you. I don't think Mr. Milovancevic will have wished to have been heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I do have a question to you, too, Mr. Milovancevic, anyway, notwithstanding my earlier indication to move to the next item. What I did want to find out from you, Mr. Milovancevic, is that whether the Defence is absolutely satisfied that from the material that they received there is nothing they want to turn into evidence by way of exculpatory material at this stage, and specifically from the material that you recently received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I presented the Defence to hand [as interpreted] at this point in time, with the proviso that I would like the Court to bear in mind the position that the Defence is in as well as the Prosecution, it's always a live process, an ongoing process and it's always a matter of identifying material, finding new material, comparing it with the facts and so on. So if we need anything like that we'll inform the Trial Chamber and tell them why this came about. Now with respect to what the Prosecutor said about disclosure, we are acquainted with that and in connection with Judge Nosworthy's question, comment, I have nothing to add. I don't think I need any comment there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. The next point the Chamber wanted to deal with relates to a couple of trial -- what do you call them? Housekeeping. Okay. First of all, the question of some maps. During the site visit, the Trial Chamber used 11 maps -- this is just by the Trial Chamber. They were not used by the parties -- depicting the locations that were visited. These maps are not marked, with the exception of one which is marked to indicate the locations. The Trial Chamber finds these maps helpful to its understanding of the case and would therefore move to have these admitted into evidence. The usher -- and may I ask her to do so, will provide both parties with copies of these maps and would the parties be so kind to review these maps now and provide the Chamber with their comments in terms of their admission. I don't know whether you have already received them or are they ready to be handed out now? I was ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My apologies. We don't have them here. Arrangements will be made that they be distributed to the parties, and may the parties just review these. They are the maps of Croatia as we know it, but we found them a little helpful. Okay. That being the case, we will skip that item now and move on to the next one, still under housekeeping. The Trial Chamber is aware of some exhibits which appear to be in duplicate in the e-court. Now, these are exhibits 127 and 220, exhibits 188 and 538, and exhibits 69 and 658. Now, although there are slight differences in the English translation, it does seem as if the B/C/S versions are virtually the same, and the question is: Do we need to have them duplicated in e-court? Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, these duplications are probably our fault, and I apologise for that, but as far as resolving this, my instinct would be to just leave things as they are and perhaps put a notation in e-court with respect to each of these exhibits that it is a duplicate of another exhibit and say which exhibit that is. The difficulty with trying at this stage to eliminate one of the duplicates is that, of course, there are references in the record to both of the versions, and it would be -- it could start to get complicated and confusing to go and to try and correct the record. So rather than trying to correct the record, I would just suggest putting a notation in e-court about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Do you have any comments to make on that, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I share the opinion of my learned friend, Mr. Whiting, since there are very few cases like that, so I don't think that complicates life too much and of course it would save us any possible problems. And I'm saying this at first sight, if I can use that term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. I would imagine, Mr. Whiting, you give same answer to -- with respect to Exhibit 902, which seems to overlap with the last page of Exhibit 923.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour. In that case, I think the -- the Defence put in Exhibit 902 and the Prosecution put in 923 with the same witness or maybe the other way around -- no, I think that's actually how it went. And, yes, I would give the same answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then in that event - and I hope this is not asking too much from registry - if there could be that notation made next to those exhibits to make sure that they are duplicates of one another. Okay. From the point of view of the Bench, all other issues that were outstanding were to be dealt with by way of decisions, and to the best of my memory all outstanding decisions have been rendered, unless I am making a mistake somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. In that event, I think that we -- all what needs to be done now is to adjourn the matter, unless anybody else has got anything else to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just -- I'm doing this a little bit on the fly, but I -- we just were handed -- handed these maps that Your Honour referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I would like to -- I don't want to make these my complete comments, but I do notice that the first map does have a date on it, it says it's from a road map from 1999. But the -- some of the other maps don't have dates on them in terms of a source, and I'm just -- it may not be relevant, but I'm wondering if that's something that is available or not available. Your Honours -- I'm looking at the second page, the third page, the fourth page, the fifth page, the sixth page. I see these have been prepared by the map unit, and I don't know if they have the date or if I'm missing it here on the sheet, and perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: From where I sit, I'm not able to answer your questions. They may or may not have dates; I really do not know. You don't -- I don't think it's something that you need to hurry about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can take your time to review the maps, Mr. Milovancevic can do the same, and you can decide when we next meet whether you accept them. And if you don't, that won't change much. Am I right to say we are supposed to stand adjourned to the 10th of January?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I believe that's correct. I don't -- if Your Honours know whether we're sitting in the morning or the afternoon, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I really wish I knew. I don't know, and I'm not going to be able to help on that in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It turns out I have another trial that's opening that day, so I'm hopefully going to be able to coordinate the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. And if they happen to sit at the same time, I think you just sort of split. Okay. Mr. Milovancevic, do you have anything to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, nothing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And you -- Mr. Martic also has nothing to raise by way of his health and his conditions in the DU? Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's just that, no, I do not have anything. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Martic. Okay. In that event, the court stands adjourned to the 10th of January, 2007. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 10th day of January, 2007

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.20 p.m.,
